claims.subject: work:rose_2004
claims.statement: The publisher presents Rose’s book as connecting settler–Indigenous reconciliation with relations to nature.
claims.qualification: Publisher-description proposal only; neither the book’s detailed method nor its reception was checked.

claims.subject: work:cruikshank_2005
claims.statement: Cruikshank treats local knowledge as produced through encounters and joins environmental change to oral and colonial histories.
claims.qualification: Specific to the Saint Elias/Yukon/Alaska inquiry; not an assertion that all Indigenous traditions are interchangeable.
claims.locator: Introduction pp. 3–4; PDF pages 1–2; lines 2–19 and 44–55

claims.subject: person:angela_sidney
claims.statement: Cruikshank credits Angela Sidney, alongside the other two named elders, with changing her thinking about glaciers.
claims.qualification: Author’s retrospective acknowledgment published in 2005 of conversations beginning in the 1970s; not a 2005 encounter or a new authorship credit.

claims.subject: work:morrison_2015
claims.statement: Morrison challenges European periodization as a global template and uses longer environmental histories to contest Anthropocene novelty.
claims.qualification: Attributed 2015 intervention; not geological consensus or evidence that she rejects anthropogenic environmental change.

claims.subject: work:davis_todd_2017
claims.statement: Davis and Todd argue that dating the Anthropocene through colonization makes dispossession and Indigenous knowledge central to its interpretation.
claims.qualification: North American standpoint explicitly bounded by the authors; their 1610 alignment is a proposal, not an accepted epoch boundary.

claims.subject: work:davis_todd_2017
claims.statement: Davis and Todd argue that Great Acceleration narratives can conceal differences in responsibility among peoples, governments and places.
claims.qualification: Specific criticism of undifferentiated attribution; not denial of measured change or rejection of all Earth-system science.

claims.subject: work:sivasundaram_2024
claims.statement: Sivasundaram advocates a global history more attentive to Earth’s materiality, developing the proposal through South Asian historiography.
claims.qualification: Explicitly neither environmental determinism nor replacement of global history by planetary history; no field-wide reception inferred.

claims.subject: work:kearns_2025
claims.statement: Kearns proposes studying Mediterranean households as sites that made environmental histories, including gendered and class-based domestic practices.
claims.qualification: Abstract checked in publisher-supplied reproduction; article-body argument and reception remain unreviewed. No Kearns–Sivasundaram exchange inferred.

claims.subject: work:nature_anthropocene_debate_2026
claims.statement: The September 2026 editorial presents competing epoch and event conceptions in a renewed Anthropocene debate.
claims.qualification: Indexed editorial excerpt only; direct page provided a preview. The 2024 IUGS rejection of a formal epoch does not end historiographical use of the term.
